topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; competency frameworks may have limited direct applicability to general workplace AI literacy in non-health sectors, though methodological approach to competency mapping could transfer.
takeaways: Use structured competency frameworks (as this review demonstrates) to map specific digital and AI skills needed in your sector—don't assume generic literacy models; tailor to your organisational context and role requirements.

Scoping reviews reveal competency gaps across diverse roles; consider conducting a similar audit in your organisation to identify which AI capabilities matter most for different employee groups before designing training.
European frameworks may differ from Australian regulatory and practice contexts; verify alignment with local standards and compliance requirements before adopting recommendations wholesale.

articles.title: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings focus on public health systems within EU contexts. Applicability to Australian health systems or non-EU countries would require consideration of different regulatory frameworks, infrastructure maturity, and workforce demographics.
takeaways: Use evidence gap analysis to identify specific digital literacy deficits within your health organisation before designing upskilling programs — avoid one-size-fits-all approaches.
Apply multiple assessment frameworks (as the study does) to triangulate digital literacy needs; single-framework assessments may miss critical capability gaps relevant to AI tool adoption.
Map current digital literacy levels across public health roles to prioritise which staff cohorts need targeted AI capability development first.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development requires interpretation and adaptation.
takeaways: Embedding AI competencies within a broader digital literacy framework (rather than in isolation) creates stronger foundational understanding — consider adopting a similar integrated approach when designing AI upskilling programs for employees.
Middle school pedagogy insights on scaffolding and competency progression could inform how you structure AI learning pathways for adults with varying technical backgrounds.
A holistic framework approach suggests combining technical AI skills with critical thinking, ethics, and real-world problem-solving rather than focusing narrowly on tool training.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on faculty development in public health education. Findings may not generalise to other sectors, industries, or non-academic settings. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI literacy can be addressed through structured professional development programs that build confidence and competence, rather than top-down mandates.
Position AI literacy training as a faculty development priority to signal institutional commitment and create peer advocates who can model AI adoption for students and colleagues.
Design curriculum interventions that help educators move from scepticism to readiness by providing hands-on experience and demonstrating practical applications within public health workflows.

articles.title: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — systematic reviews synthesise existing literature but generalisability depends on the quality and geographic diversity of included studies. The labour market context may vary significantly across countries due to different educational systems, industry composition, and economic structures.
takeaways: Data literacy is now a measurable, discrete competency in the labour market — you can assess and develop it systematically rather than treating it as innate talent, using frameworks that distinguish foundational, intermediate, and advanced levels.

Employees with formal data literacy training show improved decision-making and problem-solving in their roles — identify specific skill gaps in your team and invest in targeted upskilling programs rather than generic 'digital literacy' courses.

Data literacy gaps vary significantly by sector and role — tailor your AI capability development strategy by first mapping which departments face the steepest learning curves and which skills create the most immediate competitive advantage.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents a conceptual framework for higher education contexts, but empirical validation across diverse institutional types and geographies is unclear from the snippet alone.
takeaways: Use a four-domain model to structure AI literacy programmes in your organisation — likely covering technical understanding, ethical reasoning, strategic application, and change management.
Position AI literacy as a meta-skill that enables employees to adapt across multiple roles and contexts, not just a narrow technical competency tied to specific tools.

Consider how academic management and leadership roles specifically need AI literacy to drive institutional innovation — relevant if supporting managers in higher education or knowledge-intensive sectors.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone — the geographic scope, sample size, and sector are not indicated. Further details would be needed to determine how broadly findings apply across different organisational contexts.
takeaways: AI adoption may have contradictory effects on creativity — while it can enhance certain creative outputs, it may simultaneously constrain creative thinking in other ways; managers should monitor both benefits and potential creative limitations.

When implementing AI tools, consider how they might inadvertently reduce employee autonomy or divergent thinking; design adoption strategies that preserve space for exploratory and unconventional problem-solving.

Assess your team's creative work patterns before and after AI adoption to identify which creative capabilities are enhanced versus suppressed, allowing targeted interventions to protect valuable creative processes.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing contexts and may not generalise to other professions. Geographic scope unclear from title/snippet, though published in Nature suggests likely multi-country or single-country longitudinal design. Sample characteristics (sector-specific to healthcare) limit applicability to non-clinical workforces.
takeaways: When introducing AI tools to nursing teams, actively preserve and expand work autonomy — staff who retain decision-making authority over how they use AI tools report better wellbeing outcomes than those who experience automation-driven loss of control.
AI readiness training alone is insufficient; pair it with role redesign that maintains nurses' agency and professional discretion to achieve wellbeing benefits alongside productivity gains.

Monitor wellbeing longitudinally during AI implementation — the three-wave design suggests effects may emerge over time, so early-stage rollouts may mask later psychological impacts if autonomy is constrained.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — reflects APA perspective on US workforce conditions; may not generalise to Australian employment context, which has different labour regulations, union structures, and economic conditions.
takeaways: Acknowledge that AI-driven workplace uncertainty is a psychological stressor affecting employee wellbeing — create space in team conversations to discuss concerns about role changes and job security rather than avoiding the topic.

Design structured communication and change management processes that reduce ambiguity about how AI will affect specific roles, as uncertainty itself (not just change) drives anxiety and disengagement.

Monitor psychological safety and stress levels during AI implementation — uncertainty may amplify existing trust issues, so transparent leadership and clear timelines for transitions are essential to retention and performance.

articles.title: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition, which are not detailed in the snippet. Without knowing the geographic scope, sector focus, sample size, and methodology, it is unclear how broadly these findings on AI-enabled work systems and wellbeing apply across different organisational contexts.
takeaways: AI-enabled work systems can create both strain (e.g., increased monitoring, task displacement concerns) and resource (e.g., reduced cognitive load, automation of routine work) pathways simultaneously — assess which predominates in your context to tailor wellbeing interventions.

Design AI implementation strategies that explicitly mitigate strain risks (such as clarity on job security, autonomy in tool use) while amplifying resource benefits (such as skills development, meaningful work reallocation) to protect employee wellbeing.

Monitor wellbeing outcomes across different employee groups during and after AI adoption, as competing pathways may affect subgroups differently — use this data to refine support and change management approaches.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by focus on paternalistic leadership contexts, which are more prevalent in certain cultural settings (e.g., East Asian organisations). Findings may not transfer to organisations with participative or democratic leadership styles common in Western workplaces.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in customizing or 'crafting' how AI is deployed in their work — this strengthens collaboration more effectively than top-down implementation.
In hierarchical or paternalistic organisational cultures, pairing mentorship-style leadership with AI crafting opportunities can increase employee buy-in and collaborative use of AI systems.
Design AI onboarding programs that allow employees agency in shaping AI workflows rather than mandating rigid usage — this sense of ownership predicts better human-AI collaboration outcomes.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the snippet alone — the source (PsyPost) is a news outlet summarizing research, and critical methodological details (sample size, geography, sector, study design) are absent. The core finding about psychological safety as a mediator between AI adoption and depression requires access to the original research paper to evaluate robustness.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical lever when implementing AI tools: organisations that proactively build trust and open communication during AI rollout may buffer against negative mental health outcomes for workers.
Before deploying AI, assess and strengthen psychological safety in your team — this may be more impactful than the technical readiness of the implementation itself.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner report based on consulting experience, likely drawn from multiple client engagements across sectors, but without explicit detail on sample composition or geographic scope. Findings may be most relevant to large organisations with resources for structured change management.
takeaways: Shift framing from 'AI adoption' (technology implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (building new human behaviours and ways of working) — this reframing helps teams focus on the behavioural changes required alongside technical deployment.

Structured change approaches should target specific behaviours employees need to develop (e.g., prompt-crafting, AI output evaluation, cross-functional collaboration with AI) rather than assuming adoption will follow technology rollout.

Early identification of behavioural barriers — fear of job displacement, lack of AI literacy, resistance to new workflows — allows change leaders to design targeted interventions before adoption stalls.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — appears to be a single study testing a theoretical model; generalisability depends on sample characteristics (sector, geography, sample size) not evident from title/snippet alone. Results may not transfer across different organisational contexts or cultural settings.
takeaways: AI awareness can trigger two distinct pathways to job crafting: one through stress appraisal (threat perception) and another through resource/demand reframing (JD-R model) — managers should recognise these dual mechanisms when introducing AI tools, as employees' responses depend on which pathway activates.

Cognitive appraisal of AI (how employees interpret and evaluate the threat or opportunity) is a critical intervention point — framing AI as a tool for task redesign rather than threat can shift employees toward proactive job crafting rather than stress-driven withdrawal.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data or geographic scope. Findings and recommendations may reflect US-centric business school viewpoint and may not directly transfer to Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI adoption could trigger resistance, and design targeted communication strategies that address employee concerns about job security and skill obsolescence before rollout.

Create clear pathways for employees to develop AI-adjacent skills (e.g., prompt engineering, data interpretation, human-AI collaboration) rather than assuming AI will simply replace existing roles — this reframes AI adoption as capability-building rather than threat.

Assess your organisation's current change readiness and psychological safety before implementing AI tools; low psychological safety will amplify resistance and reduce willingness to experiment with new AI-enabled workflows.

articles.title: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — no sample size, geographic scope, or sector details provided in the snippet. Findings may not generalise across different workplace types, industries, or cultures without additional methodological information.
takeaways: Digital hoarding in workplaces has multiple distinct pathways or causes — recognising whether an employee hoards due to risk aversion, perfectionism, or information anxiety allows targeted intervention strategies rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.

Understanding the underlying motivations for digital hoarding behaviour can help you design workplace interventions (e.g. file management training, psychological safety initiatives, or clarity on data retention policies) that address root causes rather than symptoms.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry observations, but specific case details and sector applicability not evident from title alone. Findings likely skew toward large enterprises with resources for sustained AI investment.
takeaways: Structure AI transformation in phases ('horizons') rather than treating adoption as a single event — this helps teams set realistic timelines and milestones for moving from initial rollout to measurable business impact.

Identify which horizon your organization is in now and what capabilities or behaviours must shift to progress to the next — this clarifies where change management effort should be concentrated to unblock advancement.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — theoretical framework appears generalizable to knowledge workers in organizations adopting AI, but geographic scope and sample characteristics are unclear from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Job crafting behaviors shift along an approach-avoidance spectrum when AI is introduced; understanding which employees lean toward engagement versus withdrawal helps tailor adoption support strategies.
Design change management interventions that actively encourage approach-oriented job crafting (e.g., identifying new high-value tasks AI enables) rather than assuming employees will naturally adapt.
Monitor for avoidance behaviors early in AI rollout—employees avoiding AI-enabled tasks may need targeted upskilling, role clarification, or reassurance about job security to shift their response.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — snippet provides insufficient detail on the underlying study's sample, methodology, or geographic scope to assess generalisability.
takeaways: People with antagonistic narcissistic traits (dominance, entitlement, hostility) may paradoxically attract romantic partners initially, suggesting charm and confidence can override recognisable red flags.

The finding challenges the intuition that narcissism is purely a romantic liability, raising questions about why people pursue partners who research suggests are less likely to be considerate or emotionally available.
This research highlights the mismatch between initial attraction and long-term relationship quality — a reminder that first impressions shaped by charisma don't predict healthy partnerships.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — would depend on sample size, participant selection criteria, and whether findings replicate across studies. Brain imaging findings often show high variability and may not translate to behavioural predictions in real-world settings.
takeaways: Psychopathic traits correlate with measurable brain structure or activity differences — a finding that challenges the idea that psychopathy is purely a behavioural or learned phenomenon.
Brain scans alone cannot diagnose psychopathy or predict individual behaviour, making this more of a 'how fascinating!' than a practical screening tool.
The gap between what we observe in the brain and what it means for actual behaviour remains the real puzzle — biology doesn't write destiny.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — likely limited to laboratory conditions with specific personality measures; generalisability to real-world surprise events and diverse populations unknown.
takeaways: People remember surprising events differently depending on their personality — some personality types may be natural 'surprise detectors' with better recall of unexpected moments.

Your personality doesn't just affect how you react to surprises; it actually shapes what sticks in your memory, which is counterintuitive because we often assume surprise itself is the main driver of memory.

This finding is fascinating because it suggests personality is like an invisible filter on your attention and memory — explaining why two people at the same shocking event might remember completely different details.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — twin studies provide insights into genetic vs. environmental contributions but findings depend heavily on the specific population sampled and cannot be generalised across all political contexts or cultures without replication.
takeaways: Authoritarian political beliefs have a measurable genetic component, suggesting personality predispositions play a larger role than many assume — challenging the idea that politics is purely learned or ideological.

The study reveals a surprising nature-nurture blend: while genes matter, environment still shapes how those predispositions express politically, meaning upbringing and social context aren't overridden by biology.

This research is a reminder that 'opposites' in politics (authoritarian vs. libertarian) may partly reflect hardwired personality differences rather than just differing values — potentially reframing how we understand political disagreement.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely high — Cambridge research on global musical preferences suggests findings span multiple countries and cultures, though specific sample characteristics not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Your taste in music may be a more universal personality signal than you'd expect — the same genres and artists correlate with personality traits across vastly different cultures and nations.

This challenges the romantic idea that music taste is purely shaped by local culture; personality appears to drive musical choices in strikingly similar ways worldwide, which is counterintuitive and genuinely surprising.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology not provided. Generalisability depends on how diverse the wine review dataset was and whether personality assessments were validated.
takeaways: Wine review language can reveal personality traits — people's word choices when describing flavours apparently reflect broader personality patterns, showing how everyday writing reveals who we are.
AI can detect personality signals in informal, creative writing that humans might miss — an unexpected application of machine learning that bridges oenophilia and psychology.
Why it's interesting: we don't usually think of wine tasting notes as a personality window, making this a delightfully quirky intersection of food culture, language, and individual differences.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate to high — large global sample typical of PwC surveys, but representativeness varies by country and sector. Results reflect respondent perceptions rather than objective workplace conditions, and survey timing (2026) may not capture rapid changes in workplace dynamics.
takeaways: Identify which workforce fears emerge most frequently in your organisation and address them directly in team communications — unaddressed fears often manifest as reduced psychological safety and engagement.

Use global benchmarks from the survey to compare your workplace's safety climate against peers; significant gaps may indicate where targeted interventions (e.g. leader training, feedback mechanisms) could improve trust and openness.

Map survey findings to your own employee pulse data to prioritise which hope-related initiatives (e.g. career development, flexible work) will most meaningfully shift perceptions of safety and belonging.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings depend on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. Leader power distance orientation effects may vary significantly across cultural contexts, limiting applicability to all organisational settings.
takeaways: Inclusive leadership alone doesn't guarantee innovation — its effectiveness depends on whether team psychological safety is actually present; assess current safety levels before expecting innovation breakthroughs from leadership style changes.

Leaders' own cultural orientation (power distance beliefs) shapes how well their inclusive behaviours translate to team outcomes; consider coaching leaders on their underlying assumptions about hierarchy and control, not just surface-level inclusive behaviours.

Use psychological safety as a measurable intermediate outcome when implementing inclusive leadership programmes — it's the mechanism through which innovation emerges, so measure it directly rather than assuming inclusion automatically creates safety.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The model linking AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression suggests relevance across sectors, but findings may be limited by geographic scope, industry type, and sample size — requires full article review for assessment.
takeaways: AI adoption can erode psychological safety if not paired with explicit ethical leadership — leaders must actively model trustworthiness and transparent decision-making about AI to protect employee wellbeing.

Monitor employee mental health during AI implementation; depression may indicate underlying erosion of psychological safety rather than AI itself — use pulse surveys and 1:1s to surface concerns early.
Ethical leadership is a protective factor: ensure leaders communicate AI's purpose, acknowledge uncertainties, and create forums for employees to voice concerns without fear of consequences.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample characteristics, methodology, and geographic scope are not evident from the title and snippet alone. Findings may be most applicable to large, multinational organisations that engage management consulting.
takeaways: Psychological safety can reduce barriers to contribution and participation, enabling underrepresented or quieter employees to speak up and share ideas — implement team norms and leader behaviours that explicitly welcome diverse perspectives and dissenting views.

Create structured opportunities (e.g. anonymous feedback channels, round-robin contributions, psychological safety check-ins) to ensure psychological safety benefits reach all employees, not just those already confident in speaking up.

articles.title: AI technology application and employee responsibility - Nature
articles.snippet: AI technology application and employee responsibility  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a perspective piece without empirical data or specific geographic scope. Applicability depends on the full article content, which is not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Consider how to clarify employee responsibility and accountability when AI systems are deployed — ambiguity about who owns decisions can undermine psychological safety.
Design AI implementation processes that explicitly address role boundaries and decision-making authority to prevent blame-shifting or confusion during failures.

articles.title: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on theoretical argument from MIT Sloan rather than empirical research. Insights about intellectual honesty and innovation are conceptually sound but would benefit from empirical validation across different organisational contexts and geographies.
takeaways: Create norms where team members can voice dissenting views and admit knowledge gaps without fear of judgment or career consequences — this is foundational to both psychological safety and genuine innovation.
Distinguish between intellectual honesty (admitting uncertainty, changing your mind based on evidence) and blame culture — reward the former while removing punitive responses to honest mistakes.
Audit your innovation processes: do they incentivise people to present polished, certain ideas only, or do they explicitly invite 'we don't know yet' contributions and collaborative problem-solving?
